title: Why must font measurement match the drawn face?
answer: Measure the face you draw: each face and cut gives the same text its own advances

checks.question: In the first step, why does the upper marker sit 2.07 units further right than the lower one?
checks.answer: It was placed after JetBrains Mono’s width for the phrase, 6.48 units, but the words are drawn in EB Garamond, which advances 4.41 at the same size; 6.48 − 4.41 = 2.07.

checks.question: At size 0.9, which EB Garamond cut makes “Ink on paper” widest, and by how much more than Regular?
checks.answer: Bold: 4.85 units against Regular’s 4.41, 0.44 more. Italic is the narrowest, at 4.24.

checks.question: A layout measures the phrase in Regular and puts a marker 0.5 units after it, but the phrase is drawn in Bold. What happens to the gap?
checks.answer: It shrinks from 0.5 to 0.06 units: Bold advances 0.44 further than Regular at size 0.9, so the marker nearly touches the words.

cases.name: Diagram widths: Measured in EB Garamond

steps.title: Measure the wrong face and the marker lands 2.07 units too far
steps.line: Same phrase, size and 0.5-unit gap; only the measurement changes.
steps.caption: Both rows draw “Ink on paper” in EB Garamond. Each marker adds the same 0.5-unit gap, but the upper row placed it using Mono’s 6.48-unit measurement rather than Garamond’s 4.41. That puts it 2.07 units too far right. Where does the phrase’s width come from?

steps.title: A phrase’s width is the sum of its glyphs’ advances
steps.line: The ruler ends after the final glyph’s advance, not at its ink.
steps.caption: Each glyph advances the pen to the next starting point; spaces contribute movement without ink. The ruler sums those advances, ending where another glyph would begin rather than at the last ink. Measure the face you draw: each face and cut gives the same text its own advances.
steps.picture: A dimension line marked “5.88 units”; 1 label. New in this step: A dimension line marked “5.88 units”.

steps.title: Bold and italic are faces of their own, with their own advances
steps.line: Same text, size 0.9: three cuts, three widths.
steps.caption: Regular, Bold and Italic supply different glyphs and metrics. Bold here advances farther than Regular, so a marker placed using Regular’s measurement would leave less room after the bold words. The cut must agree between measurement and drawing, just as the font family must.
steps.picture: The same words in three EB Garamond cuts: Regular, advance 4.41; Bold, advance 4.85; Italic, advance 4.24. Each cut was requested and captured from its own source font.

steps.title: Measured in EB Garamond first, each box fits its word
steps.line: Under each box: how far its word was stretched to fit. Here, not at all.
steps.caption: Rayner measures Ink and Paper in EB Garamond before the layout sizes their boxes. Both words keep their natural proportions, so both stretch factors are ×1.000. Change the setting to compare a layout measured for another face.
steps.picture: Flowchart: 2 nodes, 1 link. Note: “stretched ×1.000” beside Ink; “stretched ×1.000” beside Paper.

steps.line: Under each box: how far its word was stretched to fit the width Inter would need.
steps.caption: The layout used Inter estimates, then the renderer fitted Garamond to those recorded widths. Paper needs more stretching than Ink because the width disagreement differs between words. This is the misplaced marker’s problem again: one face was measured and another drawn.
